title: Minyue
capsule: Yue (越) was a powerful state on the southeastern coast of Zhou China during the late Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, centered on its capital at Kuaiji (modern Shaoxing in Zhejiang) and controlling lands across present-day Zhejiang, Shanghai, and southern Jiangsu. Under King Goujian (r. 496–465 BC), Yue recovered from a crushing defeat by its northern rival Wu and ultimately annihilated Wu in 473 BC, after which it shifted its center northward toward the former Wu capital near Suzhou and emerged as a dominant power among the eastern states. Following Goujian's death Yue gradually declined through internal succession struggles, and around 333 BC it was conquered and partitioned by the expanding state of Chu, ending its existence as an independent kingdom.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Minyue's territorial extent is poorly attested; the Shiji and Hanshu provide political narrative but no administrative boundary data, and the dataset geometry is a scholarly reconstruction based on the distribution of archaeological Yue culture sites and the known Han commandery system that replaced it.
